Senses.Explanation: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil” is Huineng's instruction to Ming at the moment he demands the robe and the teaching. The full case immediately asks, at just that moment, for Ming's original face; later masters quote the line to place the listener under the same demand, not to prescribe a general program of suppressing moral thought. The wording belongs to a public encounter and its later re-raising.

Senses.Explanation: In the wild-fox case, 'not obscuring cause and effect' is Baizhang's turning answer; later comments question the fox's release and refuse to isolate it from the rejected companion phrase. The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing deployments and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.

Senses.Explanation: 不是心不是佛不是物 is ‘not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.’ The corpus transmits more than one explicit attribution: some witnesses introduce it with 故江西大師云 or report that 馬大師近日道 it, while the Nanquan–Zhaozhou case has 南泉云 or 南泉曰 before the same three-part formula. Later record owners raise, quote, or wield the wording in public addresses. The three coordinated negatives form one inherited utterance, but the evidence does not permit collapsing its Mazu and Nanquan transmission strands into a single origin.

Senses.PreferredTarget: not be a companion to the myriad things
AlternateTargets: the one who is not a companion to the myriad things
SearchAliases: not companion to the ten thousand things
who is not companion to all things
not partner with the myriad things
Senses.Explanation: Layman Pang’s fixed public question—who is not a companion of the ten thousand things?—is repeatedly raised afresh and answered in later records. Literally, not to be or become a companion to the myriad things. The expression is overwhelmingly recorded in the question, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The Compendium of the Five Lamps records Layman Pang asking it first of Shitou Xiqian, who covers Pang's mouth, and later of Mazu Daoyi, who answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later masters quote Pang's question as a named public case, ask it afresh, and give their own answers. Letan Huaicheng answers 'Guanyin' (觀世音菩薩). Caoshan Benji answers, 'Where did all those many people in Hongzhou city go?' (汝道洪州城裏如許多人甚麼處去). Asked directly, 'Ultimately, what is not being a companion to the myriad things?' (畢竟如何是不與萬法為侶), Yinyuan Longqi answers, 'Passing through a hundred flowers, not one leaf clings to the body' (百花叢裏過，一葉不沾身). Xingkong Zhen answers another fresh raising with 'standing openly revealed' (堂堂獨露). Yuanwu Keqin's instruction says that the ancients called someone 'the person who is not a companion to the myriad things' (古人謂之不與萬法為侶底人). Zhang Jun's preface to Yuanwu's record says that whenever Yuanwu raised this public case, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning. The entry preserves the fixed wording, its named origin, and the answers that the record attaches to it.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 446 matches in 153 files. The person-question form has 139 matches in 73 files, while the longer nominal form ending in 'the one who' has 269 matches in 117. Three passages in three files directly ask, 'What is not being a companion to the myriad things?' One text explicitly calls it the public case of not being companion to the myriad things, and one instruction uses the naming formula 'the ancients called him the person who is not a companion to the myriad things.' The distribution supports one corpus-wide fixed expression rather than a meaning restricted to Layman Pang, Shitou, or Mazu.

Senses.Explanation: In Baizhang's wild-fox case, 'not falling into cause and effect' is the old man's fatal answer; later speakers repeatedly raise and question it against 'not obscuring cause and effect.' An old man who remained after Baizhang's addresses says that in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha he had lived on that mountain. A student asked him, “does a person of great conduct still fall into cause and effect or not?” He answered, “does not fall into cause and effect” (大修行底人還落因果也無？不落因果). The record says this answer was followed by five hundred lives in a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang to give a substitute turning phrase; Baizhang answers, “does not obscure cause and effect” (不昧因果), and the old man awakens at the words. The record continues with the old man's request for a deceased monk's funeral and Huangbo's later question to Baizhang about the case. Wumen asks directly, “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?” (不落因果，為甚墮野狐？不昧因果，為甚脫野狐？). Wansong retells the same speaker turns in his commentary. A later master questions a student on the stated difference between falling and not obscuring, while an earlier lamp dialogue rebukes the cited participant's “then it does not fall into cause and effect” with “do not make a wild-jackal cry” (莫作野干鳴). The exact phrase occurs 151 times in 82 allowlisted files. A later record preserves two unnamed monks disputing the case: one says that 'not obscuring' still did not shed the fox body, while the other asks how 'not falling' ever incurred it. Chaozong's record also has an unnamed monk publicly ask why 'not falling into cause and effect' led to the fox. These are distinct later interrogations of the same case phrase, not new senses.

Senses.Explanation: Shariputra is a named disciple whom Chan masters repeatedly place inside questions, reversals, comparisons, and inherited public cases. Yongming Yanshou cites Shariputra asking for a concise statement of dependent arising. Tianyin Yuanxiu, Yuanwu Keqin, and Dahui Zonggao raise exchanges in which Shariputra questions Moon-above Woman, Subhuti, or a heavenly woman and is answered or reversed. The entry defines the figure through these Chan deployments and does not import the unattested title “foremost in wisdom.”

To roam at ease is to go or stay freely, without being tied or obstructed by what one meets. The Chan record uses it favorably but also polices the phrase against counterfeit freedom. Yongjue Yuanxian directly defines ‘what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely’ as remaining aloof and unattached amid every false scene, like a bird flying through the sky without the slightest tether and a dragon leaving the sea without the slightest obstruction (所謂逍遙放曠者，乃是於一切妄境，超然不著，如鳥飛空，而毫無所牽繫，如龍出海，而毫無所障礙). In the same address he denies that being tied by sounds, sights, wealth, or power can be called ranging freely and roaming at ease (豈曰放曠逍遙哉). Tianhuang Daowu tells Longtan Chongxin to roam at ease according to his nature, range freely following conditions, exhaust the ordinary mind, and retain no separate superior understanding (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). The Patriarchs' Hall Collection describes Danxia Tianran as delighting in clouds and waters and roaming at ease whether going or staying (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Tianyin Yuanxiu raises his staff and asks whether it is not roaming at ease and unbound; Shiyu Mingfang's community rule rejects taking crazed delusion as roaming at ease (將狂妄作逍遙者). An unnamed monk asks Lumen Fadeng about a person roaming at ease outside things, and Fadeng answers, ‘red and festering all over, unable to be supported’ (如何是逍遙物外底人；遍身紅爛，不可扶持). Yongjia Xuanjue's letter uses the ordinary motion frame ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷), which is not the place name Mount Xiaoyao. Juelang Daosheng also uses the word inside the longer title ‘Remarks on Free and Easy Wandering’; that family compound is not a fourth sense of the bare headword.
Senses.Note: Allowlisted concordance: 974 hits in 245 texts. Definition formulas yield three hits for ‘roaming-at-ease one(s)’, one direct ‘what is called roaming at ease’ formula, no exact hits for the other standard naming formulas, and seven ‘what is roaming at ease’ questions. Family counts include 53 hits for ‘roaming at ease and unbound’ (逍遙自在), 66 for ‘roam at ease according to one's nature’ (任性逍遙), nine for ‘range freely and roam at ease’ (放曠逍遙), 24 for ‘roaming at ease outside things’ (逍遙物外), and two for ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷). The 974-hit pool also contains the distinct personal title Master Xiaoyao, the place name Mount Xiaoyao, longer book-title language, and ordinary syntax; these were separated before the lexical depth count. Seven independent lexical witnesses remain after the longer-title family row is excluded. Favorable, critical, literal-motion, staff, instruction, narrative, and public-interview deployments all concern the same free-roaming action or state rather than different lexical things.
